items.t: Telefónica (BME:TEF) Updates 2026 Guidance, Is The Stock Cheap?
sum: Telefónica (BME:TEF) moved into focus after updating its 2026 guidance and releasing third quarter results, linking modest top line expectations with stronger profitability, cash generation, and a slimmer balance sheet.

The recent guidance update landed after a run of stronger news, including a return to profit over the nine months to September and a reduction in net debt of 10.8% to €25.1b. Against that backdrop, Telefónica's share price has logged a 7.97% 1 month share price return, but a 90 day share price return that declined 5.48%. The 5 year total shareholder return of 18.79% points to gains built up over a longer holding period as momentum has cooled in the near term.
Scan for other telecoms and cash generative compounders showing similar guidance and balance sheet trends by jumping into the hand picked list of solid balance sheet and fundamentals (198 results).

For Telefónica, this recent upswing sits between two stories: solid guidance and cleaner finances on one side, cooler medium term returns on the other. How does the current valuation weigh those forces?

Telefónica's last close at €3.48 sits below the analyst consensus Narrative fair value of €3.96, which implies a discount of around 12%. That view, captured in the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St, blends revenue, earnings and risk assumptions into a single long term valuation line.

The completion of large-scale portfolio optimization and monetization of non-core assets (sale of Argentina, Peru, Colombia, Uruguay, Ecuador, etc.) is reducing geographic risk and freeing up significant capital (€3 billion+). The strategy to focus on core markets (Spain, Brazil, Germany, UK) enables redeployment of resources to higher-return areas, improving free cash flow and ROCE.

That fair value of €3.96 is built using a 9.82% discount rate and analyst projections that revenue in euro terms declines modestly while profit margins improve from current loss making levels to around 7.1%. Earnings are modeled to move from a loss of €2.5b today to profit of €2.4b by around 2029, which would require the shares to trade on a P/E of 12.1x on those earnings to align with the Narrative's valuation.

items.t: Telefonica stock gains cash targets despite lower revenue outlook
sum: Telefónica reported stronger third-quarter operating performance on Thursday, November 12, while lowering its full-year revenue-growth outlook because of weaker handset sales. In its November 12 results release, the Spanish telecommunications group said revenue rose to 8.433 billion euros in the third quarter, up 2.2 percent at constant exchange rates from a year earlier.

Adjusted EBITDA increased 2.8 percent at constant exchange rates to 3.078 billion euros, while adjusted operating cash flow after leases rose 7.2 percent to 1.364 billion euros. Free cash flow from continuing operations reached 1.018 billion euros, up 220.1 percent year on year. Continuing operations generated net income of 860 million euros, an increase of 151.3 percent.

Telefónica lifted its 2026 adjusted EBITDA-growth target to slightly above 2.5 percent from a previous range of 1.5 to 2.5 percent. The company now expects adjusted operating cash flow after leases to rise by more than 3.5 percent, compared with a previous target of more than 3 percent, and raised its free-cash-flow target to around 3.1 billion euros from around 3 billion euros.

The company also introduced a service-revenue target of around 1.5 percent for 2026. At the same time, total revenue growth is now expected at 1 to 1.5 percent, down from the earlier range of 1.5 to 2.5 percent. Chief Operating Officer Emilio Gayo attributed the reduction mainly to handset sales, while saying service revenue remained solid.

Executive Chairman Marc Murtra said the group had delivered its fourth consecutive quarter of simultaneous growth in key financial metrics. He linked the performance to execution of the Transform & Grow plan and said Telefónica was raising its operating and free-cash-flow expectations.

Spain and Brazil provided the main operational support. Telefónica España increased third-quarter revenue and adjusted EBITDA by 2.6 percent each, while its churn rate fell to a record low of 0.7 percent. Telefónica Brasil lifted revenue 7.2 percent at constant exchange rates and adjusted EBITDA 9.7 percent, reaching a record 120.3 million accesses.
For the first nine months, group revenue rose 1 percent at constant exchange rates to 24.825 billion euros.

sum: Telefónica reported its third-quarter and nine-month results on Thursday, November 12, 2026, with revenue, profitability and cash generation improving across the continuing business. In its results release, the company said nine-month revenue reached 24.825 billion euros, up 2.8% at real exchange rates and 1.0% at constant exchange rates.

Adjusted EBITDA increased 4.6% at real exchange rates to 8.846 billion euros, which Telefónica described as its strongest increase in a decade. Adjusted operating cash flow after leases rose 6.1% to 4.018 billion euros, while free cash flow from continuing operations advanced 10.7% to 1.963 billion euros.

Continuing operations produced net income of 1.333 billion euros in the first nine months, an increase of 21.6% from the prior-year period. The consolidated group reported net income of 464 million euros, compared with a loss of 1.080 billion euros a year earlier, as discontinued operations recorded a net loss of 870 million euros.

The third quarter showed the same operating direction. Revenue rose 4.8% at real exchange rates to 8.433 billion euros, adjusted EBITDA increased 6.2% to 3.078 billion euros and adjusted operating cash flow after leases gained 10.6% to 1.364 billion euros. Free cash flow from continuing operations reached 1.018 billion euros, while continuing operations generated quarterly net income of 860 million euros.

Spain and Brazil were the main operating supports cited by management. Telefónica España lifted quarterly revenue 2.6% to 3.316 billion euros, while Telefónica Brasil increased revenue 15.4% at real exchange rates and adjusted EBITDA 18% in the quarter. The group ended September with 302.1 million accesses, 5% more than a year earlier.

Telefónica raised its 2026 adjusted EBITDA growth target to slightly above 2.5%, from a previous range of 1.5% to 2.5%. It also lifted the adjusted operating cash flow after leases target to above 3.5% and increased its free cash flow target to approximately 3.1 billion euros from approximately 3.0 billion euros.
The upgrade was not broad-based. The company introduced a service-revenue growth target of approximately 1.5% and reduced its total-revenue growth range to 1% to 1.5%, from 1.5% to 2.5%.

Telefónica Deutschland Holding (HMSE:O2D) Stock Looks Below Fair Value On Cash Flow
sum: Telefónica Deutschland Holding has seen its share price drift lower this year, which puts the spotlight firmly on what investors are paying for its underlying cash flows. With the stock still trading around telecom-level valuations, the open question is how well that current price lines up with the cash the business is expected to generate over time.
- The share price is down 9.4% year to date, so anyone looking at Telefónica Deutschland now is effectively reassessing what that move says about the durability and value of its future cash flows.

- The business model leans heavily on recurring mobile and broadband revenue, which can support relatively predictable cash generation but also ties the investment case to how efficiently those earnings are converted into free cash each year.
- What if you looked at Telefónica Deutschland Holding through its earnings instead? See why Telefónica Deutschland Holding's 32.6x P/E tells a different valuation story.
The issue now is whether the current Telefónica Deutschland Holding share price is appropriately aligned with what its Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) estimate suggests those cash flows are worth.
If you want a broader yardstick for Telefónica Deutschland Holding and its cash flow story, it can help to line it up against 199 high quality undervalued stocks.

The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model values Telefónica Deutschland Holding by adding up the cash it is expected to generate for shareholders over time. On the latest figures, the group is producing around €962.4 million of free cash flow over the last twelve months, which the model treats as a relatively mature base rather than a high growth starting point.

Telefonica stock heads into results test with moderate growth outlook
sum: Telefonica stock traded at 3.44 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 11:20 CET on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, 0.88 percent above the Xetra close of Monday, November 9. The move came as investors prepared for Telefónica's third-quarter results, due before the market opens on Thursday, November 12.

A preview published by Bolsamania.com on November 10 cited Renta 4 analyst Iván San Félix. Renta 4 forecasts year-on-year revenue growth of 3 percent and underlying EBITDA growth of 2 percent for the third quarter, below the consensus assumptions of 4 percent and 5 percent respectively.

Renta 4 estimates reported EBITDA at 3.067 billion euros, compared with consensus of 3.095 billion euros. The reported figure is expected to include a capital gain from the sale of the Gran Vía headquarters, making the distinction between reported and underlying performance important for investors.

Operating income is forecast at 1.334 billion euros. Attributable profit from continuing operations could reach 580 million euros, up from 342 million euros a year earlier. Including discontinued operations, Renta 4 expects attributable net profit of 566 million euros, compared with 276 million euros in the third quarter of 2025.

Spain is expected to maintain positive commercial momentum, while Brazil is forecast to deliver double-digit growth in revenue and underlying EBITDA. Renta 4 also expects a currency contribution of about 7 percent from the Brazilian real. Germany remains the main operational drag, although the negative effect should ease after customer transfers to 1&1 and an improvement in handset sales.

Renta 4 forecasts operating cash flow of 1.369 billion euros on investment of 1.002 billion euros excluding spectrum. The analysis defines this measure as underlying EBITDA after leases less capex excluding spectrum, so it is not equivalent to final free cash flow for shareholders. Net debt before leases is expected to fall by 219 million euros from the previous quarter to 25.059 billion euros, helped by asset sales.
The November 12 presentation at 10:00 CET is expected to provide the next confirmation of Telefónica's 2026 guidance.

items.t: French billionaire Xavier Niel's Millicom posts 61% revenue jump as profit halves
sum: Millicom International Cellular SA, the Latin American telecommunications group controlled by French billionaire Xavier Niel, increased third-quarter revenue by 61% after taking over former Telefónica SA businesses in Colombia, Ecuador and Uruguay, but its net profit fell by half on one-time charges.

Revenue rose to $2.28 billion in the three months to Sept. 30 from about $1.42 billion a year earlier, the company said in its results on Nov. 5. Excluding acquisitions, revenue grew 4.8%. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization increased 57.7% to $1.09 billion.

Net profit attributable to shareholders fell 49.9% to $98 million, or 58 cents a share, from $195 million, or $1.17, in the same period last year. The company has booked $149 million of restructuring costs so far this year and took a $99 million litigation settlement in Guatemala and a $32 million goodwill impairment in Costa Rica.
"We delivered another strong quarter, driven by solid execution and the commitment of our teams across Latin America," Chief Executive Officer Marcelo Benitez said.

The jump in sales reflects a string of deals that have turned Millicom, which operates under the Tigo brand, into one of the largest telecom operators in Latin America. It bought Telefónica's units in Ecuador and Uruguay in October 2025 and completed the purchase of 67.5% of Colombia Telecomunicaciones, known as Coltel, in February. It later bought the remaining Tigo Colombia shares from Empresas Públicas de Medellín and the 32.5% of Coltel held by Colombia's government.

The deals have added debt. Millicom's net debt stood at $8 billion at the end of September, or 2.53 times adjusted EBITDA, down from 2.73 times at the end of June. The company is aiming to bring that ratio below 2.5 times by the end of the year.

Equity free cash flow, the measure Millicom uses for cash available to shareholders, was $316 million in the quarter and $867 million for the year so far. The company kept its full-year target of about $1.1 billion.

How to protect yourself from phishing with mobile network security
sum: Why do we click on links even when we know the cybersecurity risks?

A link that arrives via WhatsApp. An alarming SMS from the bank. A QR code in a restaurant. A Microsoft Teams notification. An urgent email. A document someone shares while we are on the metro. A message from the boss just before going into a meeting.
We click without hesitating, without thinking, because that is how life works today: fast-paced, with multiple fronts to deal with and fires to put out at any given moment…
And yet, we have been on our guard for some time, with a constant warning in the back of our minds: do not open it, do not download it, check the sender, look carefully at the URL, be suspicious.
We make mistakes when we are in a hurry, which is quite often, when we are tired, when something looks convincing enough or simply when we are thinking about something else and let our guard down.

Our own cybersecurity requires training, common sense and good habits. That is not going to change. But I think we are asking too much if we expect people to be able to distinguish between a potential scam and something legitimate all day long, at every moment and in every situation.

Even more so now, when artificial intelligence is doing extraordinary things for all of us, but can also be used for less positive purposes, such as trying to deceive us. A phishing email no longer has to be full of spelling mistakes. It can be well written, tailored to the recipient’s context and sound entirely plausible.

Digital euro mandate puts Telefonica stock in focus
sum: Telefónica and Minsait have been selected as one of two successful tenderers to deploy communications and security infrastructure for a future digital euro. The announcement was published on Monday, November 2, 2026, and was reported by WebWire.

The consortium will connect the European Central Bank ecosystem with private and public payment facilitators, banks, fintech companies and payment service providers. Telefónica will contribute communications infrastructure through Telefónica Global Solutions and Telefónica Tech, while Minsait will provide application integration, digital identity, trust services and cybersecurity capabilities.

The planned infrastructure combines an MPLS network, SD-WAN capabilities and cybersecurity services. These systems are intended to connect different locations securely and support the exchange of information between the participants in the future digital euro ecosystem. Minsait will add API-based integration, certificates, access controls, encryption and security monitoring.

The contract is scheduled to enter into force on May 3, 2027, and runs for 10 years. The project is designed to support a digital means of payment that would complement cash across the euro area. The announcement does not disclose financial terms for Telefónica, so the immediate investment relevance lies in the company's positioning in critical communications, cloud and cybersecurity infrastructure rather than in a quantified earnings contribution.

Telefónica's next scheduled corporate milestone is the publication of its January-September 2026 results on Thursday, November 12, according to the company's shareholder and investor calendar. That report will give investors a broader basis for assessing operating trends, cash generation and the contribution potential of business-to-business technology activities.

Lula Victory Triggers Selloff in Brazilian and European Stocks
sum: Investors sold Brazilian and European equities after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated Flávio Bolsonaro in Brazil's presidential runoff on Sunday, October 25, 2026, reversing expectations of a more business-friendly government and intensifying concerns about public debt and fiscal discipline.

Brazil's Superior Electoral Court reported that Lula won 51.8% of valid votes, compared with Bolsonaro's 48.2%, with nearly all ballots counted. The result marked the first time since Brazil returned to direct elections in 1989 that a candidate won the runoff after losing the first round.

The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF fell more than 27% in premarket trading on Monday, October 26, according to reports by CNBC and Yahoo Finance. The decline put the fund on track for its steepest single-day loss since at least 2000.

Brazilian companies listed in the United States also suffered sharp losses. CNBC reported that Petrobras fell 24% in premarket trading, Itaú Unibanco dropped 26%, Ambev declined 13%, Vale lost 3.3%, and Embraer slipped 2.6%.

The selloff spread to European companies with significant Brazilian operations. Shares of Spain's Banco Santander fell nearly 4% and telecommunications group Telefónica dropped 7.2% in early trading, while AB InBev declined 3.5%, according to Yahoo Finance. Spain's IBEX 35 fell 0.3% and Portugal's PSI 20 lost 0.7%, despite gains across other European indexes.

Investors had favored Bolsonaro because his campaign promised fiscal consolidation, privatization and business-oriented reforms. His lead after the first round had reinforced expectations of a more market-friendly outcome, making Lula's victory an unexpected shock.
RBC Capital Markets analyst Benjamin Toms linked the market reaction to concerns about Lula's approach to public finances.

Cloud, Security, and Regulatory Compliance: The Technical Challenges Shaping the Evolution of the Cloud
sum: The evolution of the cloud is driven by the combination of infrastructure, security, data, artificial intelligence, and regulatory compliance to address new technological challenges.
What technical challenges are driving the evolution of cloud environments?

Cloud technologies enable the deployment and management of infrastructure that is more flexible, scalable, and tailored to the needs of each organization. Cloud technology plays a very important role among digital technologies.

Currently, cloud projects combine public, private, and hybrid environments with security, data, and artificial intelligence capabilities. This approach allows organizations to address increasingly complex technological needs from an integrated perspective.

In this context, the cloud is establishing itself as one of the key technologies for moving toward digital infrastructures that are more flexible, secure, and ready to incorporate new capabilities. Its evolution, along with fields such as artificial intelligence, data, and cybersecurity, contributes to the development of more advanced technology services and reinforces Telefónica’s role as a gateway to digital technologies, while also fostering a more innovative and competitive company.
What technical capabilities does the cloud offer public and private organizations today?
- Integration of security, data, and artificial intelligence capabilities.

The Mexican mobile market is going to look a lot different next year after AT&T and Telefónica complete the sales of their respective businesses in the country.

AT&T agreed to sell its operation, AT&T Mexico, to a consortium comprising local cable and broadcast company Grupo Televisa and investment firm Fintech Holdings for $2 billion in cash. The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals.
Shedding the Mexican business after more than ten years in the market will allow AT&T to focus capital investment on building out fiber and 5G connectivity in the US, according to the carrier.

The deal follows Telefónica's long-awaited sale of Movistar in Mexico, announced in April. The Spanish operator is selling its Mexican business for $450 million to a consortium led by telecom-as-a-service platform provider Oxio and Newfoundland Capital Management. SpaceX spectrum deal to expand its Starlink network in the US sends telecom stocks tumbling
sum: SpaceX is muscling in on US telecom territory and it's rattling the shares of top US communications giants on Friday.

SpaceX jumped as much as 4%, riding a wave of bullishness following an announcement on Thursday that the company had reached a deal to acquire the nationwide rights to a block of low frequency airwaves, a development Musk described as a "very big deal" in a post on X.

"This prime low-band spectrum addresses one of the key remaining technical gaps that will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US," SpaceX stated in its announcement.

The company said that once it receives regulatory approval, it plans to deploy a hybrid network combining its satellite and ground technology that will allow it to significantly scale device connectivity. This comes as global reliance on Starlink has grown significantly in recent years.
The news that SpaceX could expand its network to more US users sent shares of major telecom companies tumbling.
Germany's Deutsche Telekom, the majority owner of T-Mobile, and Spain's Telefónica were down 8% and 4.5% respectively in European trading.

Wall Street analysts see the deal as a major step forward for SpaceX as the company maneuvers to become the dominant satellite connectivity provider, building what it describes as "the world's most advanced mobile network."

Movistar Estudiantes Officially Unveils the 2026-2027 Season
sum: The official presentation of Movistar Estudiantes’ 2026-27 season brought together players, coaching staff, academy teams, sponsors, institutions, media representatives and fans this Monday at the Espacio Movistar in the Telefónica Building. Held on Madrid’s Gran Vía, the event marked the start of a new chapter for the club, shaped by a new institutional era and a message that will accompany the team throughout the season: Indestructibles.

Hosted by José Ajero and Iyi Martín, the presentation began by looking back at the club’s recent history. One of the highlights of the event was a tribute to Jayson Granger following his retirement from professional basketball. The Uruguayan player arrived at Ramiro at the age of 15, developed through the club’s academy and made his ACB debut wearing the Estu jersey before going on to enjoy a long and successful national and international career. Movistar Estudiantes honoured his legacy and connection with the club with a special video and his appearance on stage.

The event also paid tribute to those who have led the club in recent years. Ignacio Triana and Vicente Olivenza, Movistar Estudiantes’ principal shareholders during the past seasons, were recognised for their commitment to and involvement with the club.

The presentation then moved on to the unveiling of a new institutional phase for Movistar Estudiantes, led by its new majority shareholder, Diego Megía, who addressed attendees to share the vision for this new chapter while highlighting the club’s identity and values.

On the court, three senior teams will take centre stage this season. items.t: Telefónica (BME:TEF) Is Back In The Spotlight, What Is Driving Attention?
sum: Telefónica (BME:TEF) drew fresh attention after its latest share price closed at €3.75, with recent returns mixed between the past week, month, past 3 months and year.

Recent trading has tilted in Telefónica's favour, with the latest move taking the share price to €3.75 and a 7.79% year to date share price return. However, the 1 year total shareholder return declined 11.5%, which suggests short term momentum is picking up while longer term holders have had a tougher run.
Scan Telefónica alongside other potential rebound stories by checking our curated list of 169 high quality undervalued stocks that combine solid fundamentals with room for sentiment to shift.

Telefónica has edged higher in the short term, while longer term investors are still in the red. Does that recent shift leave more upside for new buyers, or is most of the easy risk reward already gone as valuation comes into focus?

Against Telefónica's last close at €3.75, the most followed narrative pegs fair value at about €3.96, which implies a modest discount and puts the focus squarely on how the business reshapes its portfolio and cash generation over time.

The completion of large-scale portfolio optimization and monetization of non-core assets (sale of Argentina, Peru, Colombia, Uruguay, Ecuador, etc.) is reducing geographic risk and freeing up significant capital (€3 billion+). The strategy to focus on core markets (Spain, Brazil, Germany, UK) enables redeployment of resources to what are viewed as higher-return areas, with an emphasis on free cash flow and ROCE.
Still, Telefónica carries high leverage and faces pressure in mature markets like Spain and Germany. This could undermine the current undervalued narrative if progress stalls.

items.t: Telefónica, new Official Partner of Espai Barça
Telefónica to Share How Risk-Based Aftersales Planning Protects Mission-Critical Service Levels
sum: At LogiAftersales 2026, Telefónica will share practical insights on balancing service availability, and inventory investment across complex spare parts networks

BOSTON, MA, UNITED STATES, September 17, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- ToolsGroup today announced that Telefónica SA will share how risk-based aftersales planning can help global service organizations protect mission-critical availability without tying up unnecessary capital in spare parts inventory. The session will feature Michel Hasenclever, Head Global Supply Planning at Telefónica SA, and will focus on practical ways to reduce service-level risk across complex, multi-echelon service networks.

Aftersales organizations are facing a sharper planning challenge as intermittent demand and long-tail SKU portfolios collide with global supply disruptions and rising service expectations, making spare parts inventory decisions more complex than ever.A single missing part can affect availability, service commitments, and customer trust, while excess inventory can constrain working capital and add operational cost.

In his session, Hasenclever will discuss how organizations can use probabilistic planning, multi-echelon inventory optimization (MEIO), and data-driven inventory policies to make more resilient decisions across distributed service networks. The discussion will highlight how risk-aware planning helps teams move beyond averages, quantify service trade-offs, and align inventory strategies with both customer commitments and business performance.

“In aftersales, every inventory decision is a service decision,” said Hasenclever. “When demand is intermittent and networks are complex, planning based on averages is no longer enough. Organizations need to understand the probability of risk, the business impact of stockouts, and the value of each inventory investment so they can protect availability where it matters most.”

“Telefónica’s perspective reflects a broader shift in supply chain planning: companies need to understand risk, not just forecast demand,” said Sean Elliott, CEO of ToolsGroup. “In volatile environments, better outcomes come from better decisions. Organizations need planning systems that continuously evaluate trade-offs, adapt as conditions change, and help teams act with confidence.”

items.t: Telefónica shares fall due to the ex-dividend effect, discounting €0.15 per share
sum: Investing.com - Telefónica shares (BME:TEF) are leading the losses on the Ibex 35 this Tuesday, down nearly 4%, a move that is entirely due to a technical correction and not to any deterioration in the company's fundamentals: Today, June 16, 2026, the shares are trading ex-dividend, meaning the market has automatically discounted the €0.15 gross dividend that the telecom company will pay its shareholders next Thursday, June 18, from the price.

This phenomenon, known as the dividend opt-out effect, is purely an accounting matter. As explained by XTB, when a stock reaches its ex-dividend date, the opening price is adjusted downward by an amount equivalent to the gross dividend, reflecting that buyers from that day forward are no longer entitled to that payment. With a payment of €0.15 on a previous share price that yielded a dividend yield of 3.8%, the correction observed in the charts is consistent with that discount. There is, therefore, no negative market sentiment regarding the stock.

Despite Telefónica's weight in the Spanish index, the Ibex 35 manages to remain in positive territory: the index is trading around 19,098.66 points, up 0.35%, within an intraday range of 19,033.97 to 19,121.46 points, according to data from Investing.com. The index's gain over the past twelve months exceeds 37%, placing it just shy of its 52-week high of 19,152 points.

Today's payment is also a milestone with strategic implications for the operator's shareholders. This is the final semi-annual dividend under the dual-payment scheme that Telefónica had maintained for years: two payments of €0.15 each, equivalent to €0.30 gross annually. In November 2025, the company announced a 50% cut in its dividend policy as part of its "Transform & Grow" strategic plan, aimed at cost savings and long-term value creation. From now on, Telefónica will make a single annual payment of €0.15, with the next one scheduled for June 2027.
To cover this second installment of the 2025 dividend, Telefónica will disburse approximately 850 million euros, according to Expansión.

items.t: Combating Fraud: collaboration, consumer education and law enforcement
sum: The rise in fraud and scams is a major and growing concern, prompting stakeholders across the digital ecosystem to step up their efforts. Fraud is defined by the UK Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) as “the act of gaining a dishonest advantage, often financial, over another person.” A scam, according to the Cambridge Dictionary, is “a dishonest plan for making money or gaining an advantage, especially one that involves tricking people.” As many languages do not distinguish between these terms, they are used interchangeably here.

Online fraud is a global and organised criminal threat:Online and ICT-enabled fraud has evolved into industrial-scale criminal operations, often run by transnational organised crime groups targeting victims across borders. In the UK, fraud already accounts for around 40% of all crimes, largely driven by online methods. This share is expected to grow further due to the transnational nature of crime and the increasing democratisation of AI tools, yet it receives less than 2% of police resources.

Fraud undermines trust in the digital economy. Anyone can fall victim to scams. It affects people of all ages, particularly vulnerable and less informed groups. Criminals are increasingly exploiting the human factor through social engineering techniques. For consumers and businesses, this threat can result in financial loss, significant emotional distress, or a loss of trust in digital services, ultimately creating barriers to the adoption of beneficial technologies.

The global financial cost of cybercrime, including fraud, is projected to rise from USD 9.22 trillion in 2024 to USD 15.63 trillion by 2029. Recent research by the Global Anti-Scam Alliance estimates that in the 12 months to October 2025 an estimated USD 442 billion was lost to scams worldwide.

The UN Global Summit on Fraud took place on 16–17 March in Vienna. Organised by UN Office on Drugs and Crime and INTERPOL, the Summit featured strong participation from international organisations, governments across regions, and private sector signalling political momentum for the fight against fraud and scams.

What is the Digital Services Act or DSA?
sum: - Signed in 2022, the Digital Services Act applies stricter rules to very large online platforms and search engines, defined as those with more than 45 million active users.
The Digital Services Act, also known as the DSA, is a European Union regulation that seeks to provide legal coverage for the regulation of online platforms and services.

Its main objective is to help create a digital space that is safer, fairer and more transparent for all citizens, by forcing companies to take responsibility for illegal content and protecting fundamental rights.

As explained on the official EU website, this law aims to ‘establish a clear set of rules across the EU’, while ‘also allowing smaller platforms, SMEs and start-ups to expand in Europe, fostering innovation, growth and competitiveness’.
The principle governing the DSA is that what is illegal in the physical world should also be illegal in the digital world and will apply to all online intermediaries providing services in the EU.

This regulation was proposed by the European Commission and subsequently negotiated and signed by the European Parliament and the Council of the EU – some of the main institutions of the European Union – on 19 October 2022.

For citizens as a whole, the Digital Services Act aims to protect digital rights such as transparency in the criteria for content removal, the ability to appeal certain content moderation decisions, and the ability to report illegal content, services or goods through easy-to-use mechanisms.

items.t: Consolidation and digital sovereignty: an urgent European agenda
sum: For more than twenty years, I have had the opportunity to follow the regulatory evolution of telecommunications in Europe from different professional perspectives, not only from Telefónica. During this time, I have seen how a well-intentioned vision – maximising retail competition at all costs- has had its merits, but also led to fragmentation that is now taking its toll.
The lack of scale limits investment and Europe’s digital competitiveness

Oliver Wyman’s Capital Currents report illustrates this starkly: the average European operator serves 5 million customers; the average US operator, 107 million; and the average Chinese operator, 467 million. This difference in scale explains why Europe invests only €109 per capita annually in telecommunications, compared to €174 in the United States – a 37% gap that results in slower rollouts, less resilient networks and reduced capacity to compete in advanced digital services.

Connectivity is no longer just another service; it is the critical infrastructure underpinning productivity, scientific innovation, the green transition and the continent’s security. Without operators of sufficient scale, Europe will not achieve robust standalone 5G, universal enterprise fibre, sovereign data centres or AI platforms developed and governed within Europe.
In a world where technology defines geopolitical power, this is a risk we cannot afford.
Consolidation as the key to achieving competitiveness, sustainability and cohesion in Europe

Fortunately, the regulatory winds are shifting. The reports by Mario Draghi and Enrico Letta have placed dynamic efficiency – the sustained ability to invest and innovate – at the heart of the debate, and the European Commission has made boosting competitiveness and technological sovereignty one of its top political priorities.
